claims.text: FCC/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit a transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition during intermediate thermal aging.
Percolation of ordered B2 domains drives the intermediate-aging loss of ductility.
Coherent local chemical orders pin dislocations and restrict slip transmission.
Dissolution of LCOs at higher temperatures restores ductility.
A transition to incoherent interfaces at higher temperatures restores ductility.
The initial alloy contains FCC and a continuous or semi-continuous ordered B2 matrix.
A continuous ordered B2 structure is associated with high strength and limited ductility.
The limited ductility is caused by the ordered nature of the B2 phase.
Relevant intermediate aging temperatures are approximately 500–700 °C.
Impurity segregation and grain coarsening are absent in the proposed aging regime.
Deformation occurs by dislocation slip in FCC and by shearing or climb in B2.
Aging changes phase boundaries from coherent to semi-coherent or incoherent states.
Intermediate-temperature aging intensifies B2 ordering or forms LCOs.
The resulting ordered-domain network impedes dislocations through order hardening and coherent-interface pinning.
Dislocation impediment by the ordered-domain network causes brittle fracture.
At higher temperatures, thermal energy overcomes ordering energy or promotes interface decohesion or coarsening.
Reduced ordering or interface barriers permit dislocation transmission and recover ductility.
Ductility falls from a high initial value to near zero at intermediate aging temperatures and then recovers at higher temperatures.
The embrittlement regime is bounded by temperatures at which LCOs are stable and percolating but have not dissolved or coarsened into incoherent precipitates.
Transition temperatures depend on alloy-specific ordering energies and diffusion coefficients.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as already having a continuous or semi-continuous ordered B2 matrix, while the mediator and mechanism attribute embrittlement to aging-induced formation of a percolating ordered-domain network. The hypothesis does not distinguish pre-existing B2 continuity from the proposed new percolation event.
